text: Running on a simulator feels instant: submit, wait a fraction of a second, get results back in the same breath. Real IBM Quantum hardware is a shared resource used by many people at once, which means your job doesn't just run — it waits in line first.

Jobs on real hardware go through a Runtime primitive, like SamplerV2 for measurement outcome distributions. Submitting returns a job object immediately, before the job has actually run — submission is asynchronous, and job.job_id() is your handle on this specific submission.

A submitted job moves through states you can poll: QUEUED, waiting behind other jobs on the same backend; RUNNING, currently executing; DONE, finished successfully; or ERROR or CANCELLED. Because the backend is shared, QUEUED is often where a job spends most of its real-world wall-clock time — not because anything is broken, but because other users' jobs are ahead of yours. And because jobs run server-side, you can close your session entirely and retrieve the same job later by its ID, even from a different machine.

Here's a real diagram from IBM's own Qiskit documentation showing how a batch actually works: classical preprocessing for each job happens in parallel, then all jobs go to the QPU, which stays locked for the whole batch from the first job's arrival to the last job's finish.

The alternative is a session, which reserves the QPU across a window of jobs with an interactive time-to-live between them — a different tradeoff, useful when jobs genuinely depend on each other's results rather than just needing to run back-to-back.

Each job submission effectively gets its own place in the shared queue. If you have ten circuits, ten separate jobs means ten separate queue positions. Runtime primitives accept a list of circuits in one run call, submitting all of them under one job ID, in one queue position — almost always faster in practice, and considerate of the shared resource everyone else is waiting on too.

Next lesson looks at what actually comes back once a job is done on real hardware — how a genuinely noisy result differs from everything you've seen in simulation so far, and the real signature to watch for.
